 At Sonia's book launch, Gandhis open up about love, loss, and bad chicken

 Print Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra with her mother Sonia Gandhi at the book release event NEW DELHI: "And listen, if you want to fall in love, go to Varsity Restaurant in Cambridge. But never eat the chicken chasseur, okay?" Rahul Gandhi jokingly delivered this piece of advice at the launch of his mother Sonia Gandhi 's memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love', in Delhi on Monday. Years after hearing the story about his parents' first meeting in Cambridge, he recounted how he went to the Varsity Restaurant with his girlfriend to see where they had met. When Rahul told the man at the entrance that his parents had met there, the man said he knew exactly who they were and recommended the chicken chasseur from the menu. However, the meal did not live up to its romantic legacy. Rahul contrasts his parents' memories of the restaurant with his own experience. "They seem to remember that the food was fantastic. The food's horrible!" he said as the audience laughed. The anecdote was part of a series of family recollections the leader of the opposition shared after saying he had been instructed to avoid politics. However, many read a political subtext into the seating arrangements. In the front row was an array of opposition leaders such as Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav; Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee; National Conference president Farooq Abdullah; Supriya Sule of NCP-SP; Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren; and Tamil Nadu CM C Joseph Vijay. Also in the front row was former Punjab CM Captain Amarinder Singh, who left Congress in 2021 following a bitter falling-out with the Gandhis. Rahul name-checked Amarinder and mentioned that he had seen his parents fight only once. Rajiv Gandhi was speaking to Amarinder on phone when Sonia tried several times to tell him something. Rajiv was stressed and eventually got angry. "We saw them argue many times, but that was the only time we ever saw them fight," Rahul said. Sonia Gandhi too kept the conversation away from politics. Asked why she chose to write a memoir when she had guarded her privacy fiercely in the past, she said she wanted to set the record straight about her family amid "unreal stories" woven around them. "So much has been said about my mother-in-law, husband, son, daughter, and myself; and most of it is unreal. It has really nothing to do with the way we are. Stories are woven around you, untruths are woven around you, and hurtful things are said which are nowhere near the truth. And I thought, well, perhaps this was a way of bringing out my feelings, what I know of my family, and maybe people will be open to listening to my story too," the Rajya Sabha MP said. She recalled feeling like an outsider when she first moved to India, conscious of making mistakes. She connected that experience to Indian women who enter a new family after marriage and have to adjust to its ways. The memoir's title, she said, reflected "the effort to be accepted and to belong, to finally belong." While she recounted a story of how she and Rajiv would go to India Gate to have ice cream (she had a favourite Sardarji ice cream vendor), Rahul spoke of his parents' affection and a habit he had assumed was common in every home: "Every meal there would be Papa and on Papa's lap there would be Mama." He said he realised it was unusual only when he visited friends' homes. Join conversation

 But things changed after the assassinations of Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi, he said, "The fun-loving mother, the smiling mother disappeared." Sonia, once an extrovert, withdrew into herself. Rahul also spoke of his mother's resilience in the face of cancer, saying he had never seen her afraid or back down. He ended by telling her how proud he believed Rajiv would have been of her: "Mummy, Papa loved you. But I cannot even tell you how proud he would be of you."
